input.prompt:
You are an engineer on the Fortress revival, a project that revives Sun's Fortress language (an interpreter and a partial JVM compiler, built with ant). Work only in /home/user/blind-opus, a git worktree of the repository at an older commit, made for you; do not read anything under /home/user/fortress or any other directory of /home/user, and do not read session transcripts or scratchpads. Do not commit or push. Do not include any model identifier in what you write. Your final text is your deliverable.

This worktree holds what an earlier attempt left when it was stopped mid-way: a `ProjectFortress/build` that may be incomplete and a `wt-sim/` directory. Account for them in what you measure. Never let one tool call wait longer than about 240 s: a long command goes in the background with a log and you poll it in calls that each return within 240 s.

## The situation

A batch pipeline runs several "rungs" in parallel, each by one worker in its own git worktree of this repository (made with `git worktree add`), so that rungs do not collide. Each rung edits Fortress (Java or Scala sources, or the Fortress library under `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`), writes a test, and runs it. After each worker, a second agent, the skeptic, checks the rung in the same worktree, and writes and runs its own small Fortress programs, sometimes against the old code (the batch's base commit) and the new. Up to four rungs run per batch, two agents at a time, and there are many batches ahead.

Each worktree must be able to compile and run Fortress programs. Measured on this machine:
- `ProjectFortress/build` (the compiled Java and Scala classes, about 40 MB) is gitignored, so a fresh worktree has none; `ant compileAll` takes about 80 s.
- The compiled library lives under `default_repository/caches/` (gitignored except `global.map`). A fresh worktree with the build copied in recompiles the library components cold, about 145 s (AnyType 21 s, CompilerBuiltin 104 s, CompilerLibrary 17 s, CompilerAlgebra 2 s, CompilerSystem 1 s), with `bin/fortress compile` in a fixed library order (`explorations/repo-internals.md`).
- The analysed cache's file names carry a hash of the source file's absolute path: `NamingCzar.deCaseName` builds each name as `<ApiName>-<hex of sourcePath.hashCode()>` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/NamingCzar.java`, around lines 243-260), so the main tree's cache files have other names than a worktree's would.
- A worktree whose `ProjectFortress/build` is a symlink to the main tree's makes `ProjectProperties` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/repository/ProjectProperties.java`) resolve its home to the main tree, so it silently compiles the main tree's sources.

The director's goal, in his words: no repeated builds; "Are we still keeping separate skeptics that are sharing some common build phase?"; reuse the cached, already-compiled library rather than rebuilding it in every worktree.

## The question

What is the cheapest way to give each worktree a ready build and a ready library cache, and to let a skeptic run its own small programs against both the old and the new code, with no build repeated? Propose the design. You may measure for up to about 45 minutes in /home/user/blind-opus (build it, copy, experiment), bounding every command's output and running long commands in the background with a log (the Bash tool stops at 10 minutes). Environment: `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64; export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH; export FORTRESS_HOME=/home/user/blind-opus; unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`.

Return, under 800 words: the designs you considered, what you tried and measured (with times), what worked and what did not, your recommended recipe step by step with its cost per worktree, and anything you would want to try next.

You are an engineer on the Fortress revival, a project that revives Sun's Fortress language (an interpreter and a partial JVM compiler, built with ant). Work only in /home/user/blind-opus, a git worktree of the repository at an older commit, made for you; do not read anything under /home/user/fortress or any other directory of /home/user, and do not read session transcripts or scratchpads. Do not commit or push. Do not include any model identifier in what you write. Your final text is your deliverable.

This worktree holds what an earlier attempt left when it was stopped mid-way: a `ProjectFortress/build` that may be incomplete and a `wt-sim/` directory. Account for them in what you measure. Never let one tool call wait longer than about 240 s: a long command goes in the background with a log and you poll it in calls that each return within 240 s.

## The situation

A batch pipeline runs several "rungs" in parallel, each by one worker in its own git worktree of this repository (made with `git worktree add`), so that rungs do not collide. Each rung edits Fortress (Java or Scala sources, or the Fortress library under `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`), writes a test, and runs it. After each worker, a second agent, the skeptic, checks the rung in the same worktree, and writes and runs its own small Fortress programs, sometimes against the old code (the batch's base commit) and the new. Up to four rungs run per batch, two agents at a time, and there are many batches ahead.

Each worktree must be able to compile and run Fortress programs. Measured on this machine:
- `ProjectFortress/build` (the compiled Java and Scala classes, about 40 MB) is gitignored, so a fresh worktree has none; `ant compileAll` takes about 80 s.
- The compiled library lives under `default_repository/caches/` (gitignored except `global.map`). A fresh worktree with the build copied in recompiles the library components cold, about 145 s (AnyType 21 s, CompilerBuiltin 104 s, CompilerLibrary 17 s, CompilerAlgebra 2 s, CompilerSystem 1 s), with `bin/fortress compile` in a fixed library order (`explorations/repo-internals.md`).
- The analysed cache's file names carry a hash of the source file's absolute path: `NamingCzar.deCaseName` builds each name as `<ApiName>-<hex of sourcePath.hashCode()>` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/NamingCzar.java`, around lines 243-260), so the main tree's cache files have other names than a worktree's would.
- A worktree whose `ProjectFortress/build` is a symlink to the main tree's makes `ProjectProperties` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/repository/ProjectProperties.java`) resolve its home to the main tree, so it silently compiles the main tree's sources.

The director's goal, in his words: no repeated builds; "Are we still keeping separate skeptics that are sharing some common build phase?"; reuse the cached, already-compiled library rather than rebuilding it in every worktree.

## The question

What is the cheapest way to give each worktree a ready build and a ready library cache, and to let a skeptic run its own small programs against both the old and the new code, with no build repeated? Propose the design. You may measure for up to about 45 minutes in /home/user/blind-opus (build it, copy, experiment), bounding every command's output and running long commands in the background with a log (the Bash tool stops at 10 minutes). Environment: `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64; export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH; export FORTRESS_HOME=/home/user/blind-opus; unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`.

Return, under 800 words: the designs you considered, what you tried and measured (with times), what worked and what did not, your recommended recipe step by step with its cost per worktree, and anything you would want to try next.

content.text:
P1 asks one question. In the interpreter, what type should `T` become in a generic call when nothing at the call fixes it and its bound refers to `T` itself?

- **The case:** `SUM` is declared `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]`. Its bound names `T` inside itself, which is called an F-bound. When a program writes `SUM[i <- 1#100] i` without `[\ZZ32\]`, nothing tells the interpreter what `T` is.
- **What happens today:** the interpreter sets `T` to `Bottom`, the empty type, and the run crashes. This has been so since batch 6's flattening made `SUM` F-bounded. The walk smoke test from CLAUDE.md (`explorations/claude_demo.fss`) and 18 of the team's 21 demos die this way.
- **Why the paper's rule doesn't settle it:** your rule from the POPL 2019 paper says a parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, never `Bottom`. Batch 9 built that for plain bounds. But the paper's type system doesn't allow a method's type parameter to appear in its own bound, so it says nothing about F-bounds. This is the other half of ledger row 424.
- **What P1 does:** it lists every way the language and library offer. Examples are inferring `T` from the generator's element type, the library's existing witness `typecase` device, replacing the self-reference in the bound with the argument's type, falling back to `Any`, and refusing the call as the compiled checker does. It measures each way on the smoke test, the 18 demos, the tests that use an unwritten `SUM`, and the interpreter suite.
- **Where the answer goes:** a Fable judgement chooses among the ways. If that lands before batch 10 launches, rung W builds it. If not, W goes ahead without it and this waits for a later batch.

It is the "later work" your earlier decisions left open. You approved writing the static argument (`SUM[\ZZ32\]`) in microGPT's own lines. For the demos you said "Let's not touch them and we'll make them run later."

content.text:
No. Resume is what you meant, and I tried it first, but it isn't available, so relaunching was the only option.

- **What I tried first:** a message to each of the six stopped workers asking it to continue from where it stopped. That is a resume, with the worker keeping everything it had read. The harness refused all six with: "was stopped by the user and won't be resumed ... only launch a new agent if the user explicitly asks". A worker killed by a stop can't be resumed at all.
- **What a relaunch is:** a new worker with the same brief. It starts with nothing in its head, so it has to re-read to catch up. Anything the old worker left on disk is kept, and I pointed each new one at it: P1's measured way 1 and its base build, the archaeology's extracts, the review's edit to the record.
- **What the difference costs:** the re-reading, roughly what each worker had spent getting up to speed. That is a few hundred K for the review and for each Sonnet worker, and less for the blinded pair. P1's predecessor had about 300K in context. A resume would not have been free either: after more than 5 minutes stopped, its whole context would have been re-sent anyway.
- **The one thing it broke:** I told the new workers to read their predecessor's transcript to see where it stopped. That is what tripped the Fable review on the safety filter. The third start reads no transcript.

So your "relaunch" was the explicit word the harness required. FACTS now records that a worker stopped this way can only be relaunched.

**Is the cache 5 minutes for workers and 1 hour for this thread?** Yes, and it is a fact, not something I derived. The API labels every cache write with how long it lives:
- This session's writes are all labelled 1 hour (`ephemeral_1h`).
- Every worker's writes are labelled 5 minutes (`ephemeral_5m`), P1's included.
- The platform's own instructions to me also say this session uses a 1-hour cache.

My first estimate came from P1's waits of 8 to 13 minutes, each followed by a full context rewrite. The labels confirm it. Both points are now in FACTS.

**Can P1 keep its cache warm?** Yes, without any special mechanism:
- Its long runs go in the background, and it checks on them with commands that each return within 4 minutes.
- Each check is a call that reads the cache and keeps it alive. A read costs next to nothing; only the new few hundred tokens are written.
- So an hour of waiting is about 15 cheap checks instead of rewriting 300K every 10 minutes.
- Its new brief tells it exactly this, with the command to use. I don't rely on a worker being able to get a background ping the way I can; short checks do the same job.

**So far:** the new P1 has made 50 calls, the longest gap between them 38 seconds. It has written 143K, all of it the reading it needed to catch up, with no rewrites. Its long runs haven't started yet. I'll check its gaps once the first one is under way.

lastPrompt: > Batch 10 should cost about what batch 9 did, around 6M.  Didn’t we just optimize the cache reuse? Wouldn’t that drop the cost?

content.text:
No. The cache reuse is already in batch 9's figure, because batch 9 was the first batch to use it.

- **What it saved:** mostly machine time, about 1.5 hours across the batch. Builds were never a large token cost. Batch 8's repeated builds and second gate wrote about 0.23M while agents waited on them.
- **The cache-expiry waste:** it doesn't happen inside a batch. I just measured batches 8 and 9: no agent waited longer than the cache lasts, so there were zero context rewrites. The script's 270-second cap on waits works. P1's 6.6M happened only because I briefed it by hand without that cap.
- **Where a batch's tokens actually go:** agents reading code and context and thinking. In batch 9:
  - rung workers 2.7M
  - skeptics 1.2M
  - two refusal-and-repair chains 1.4M
  - landing 1.6M
- **What may lower batch 10:**
  - the narrower grounds for a skeptic's refusal, built after batch 9 (about 0.5M per refusal of the kind batch 9 had)
  - the cut to W's 62K-token briefing
  - no VM restart this time (about 0.5M in batch 9)

  That puts my honest estimate at about 5.5M to 6M, not much lower. Cutting deeper means changing what the agents read and how many check each rung, which is the allocation study's question.

The first result of the blinded test is in.

Fable, given the tree as it was on 09-17 and your goal, found the answer we built last night:
- **The design:** copy the build into the worktree, copy the cache, and rename each cache file to the hash of its new path. About 5 seconds per worktree.
- **What it cost:** about 15 minutes and 0.24M tokens over its two starts.
- **Two things we don't do yet, both measured:**
  - A skeptic can run the old code against one shared, read-only base build with a private cache folder. Each rung then needs no copy of the base.
  - `ant compileAll` can be told not to delete the cache, so a Java edit no longer forces the 145-second library rebuild. Its own caveat: a compiler change that alters how the library compiles still needs that rebuild.
- **Caveat on its timings:** the stopped attempt had already finished the build, so this run didn't pay for it. The design question isn't affected.

The Opus run is still going; I'll compare the two when it reports.

# Blinded test, Opus worker (relaunch), final report as handed back 2026-10-03 ~05:25 UTC
# Worktree /home/user/blind-opus at 3f3f766a2. Its first start (stopped at 04:49) had left wt-sim/a holding a relocated cache, which this run found and validated.

## Recommendation: copy the build, relocate one shared library cache, and give the skeptic no build of its own

Every timing below was taken while other sessions kept the 4-core machine at a load average of 5–8, so the times are inflated.

**Designs considered**
1. Each worktree builds everything itself (61–80 s build, 145–194 s library).
2. Symlink `ProjectFortress/build` to the base tree's build.
3. Copy the build and recompile the library cold.
4. Copy the build and **relocate** the base tree's compiled caches. Recommended.
5. For old-code runs, use the base tree itself with a private cache directory.

**What I measured**
- A no-op `ant compileAll` takes 61 s and is never a no-op: scalac always recompiles every Scala source. `compileAll` depends on `cleanCache`, which deletes `default_repository/caches` (tracked `global.map` included); the first run wiped the earlier attempt's library cache, rebuilt cold in 194 s (AnyType 27, CompilerBuiltin 135, CompilerLibrary 25, CompilerAlgebra 3, CompilerSystem 3.5).
- Creating a worktree (separate-index checkout as a stand-in for `git worktree add`): 1.6 s, 222 MB. Copying the 40 MB build: 0.17–0.3 s.
- Trap: checkout mtimes make `Fortress.ast` look newer than the generated AST sources and the copied `OperatorStuffGenerator.class` newer than `Operators.java`; one edited Java file then cost 104 s (1,071 AST sources regenerated identically, 1,073 files recompiled).
- Fix: copy the base tree's mtimes onto the tracked files (0.17 s for 10,506 files), then `cp -a` the build and `.dependencies`: the same one-file edit cost 74 s, 1 file compiled, nothing regenerated; the remaining ~60 s is scalac.
- Relocation: rename each cache file with the new path's hash and rewrite the embedded absolute paths, over the analysed, interpreter and interpreter-parsed caches, `bytecode_cache` and `nativewrapper_cache` copied unchanged: 0.1–0.3 s. In the relocated worktree: compile 3.4–4.6 s, run 0.7 s, interpreter 9 s, no library cache file rewritten. Without it: interpreter first run 38 s, compiler path 145–194 s library build.
- Library edits are incremental: a comment added to `CompilerLibrary.fss` recompiled CompilerLibrary 30 s, CompilerAlgebra 1.3 s, CompilerSystem 2.2 s; CompilerBuiltin and AnyType untouched (cold: 194 s).
- Old-code runs: `FORTRESS_HOME=<base>` plus `FORTRESS_CACHES=<private copy of the shared cache>` (0.01 s, no relocation); compile 3.4 s, run 0.7 s; base cache md5-identical before and after.
- Symlinked build confirmed broken without `FORTRESS_AUTOHOME` (a compile wrote into the base tree's cache); with it, `ant` in the worktree would still write through the symlink. Copying costs 0.2 s, so a symlink saves nothing.

**Recommended recipe**
Once per batch, in base tree B at the base commit (4–5 min, only when the base changed): 1. `ant compileAll` (61–80 s; step 2 must follow). 2. Library compile in the fixed order (145–194 s). 3. Warm: compile and run one test program, one through the interpreter (~45 s). 4. Copy `B/default_repository/caches` to a frozen shared cache, minus the test program's entries and `logs` (0.1 s). B read-only for the rest of the batch.
Per rung worktree W (about 2.2 s, 300 MB): 5. `git worktree add --detach W <base>`. 6. `mtimesync.py B W` (0.17 s). 7. `cp -a` B's `ProjectFortress/build` and `ProjectFortress/.dependencies` into W (0.2 s). 8. `rm -rf W/default_repository/caches/*_cache`, then `relocate.py <shared cache> W/default_repository/caches B W` (0.2 s).
Worker: a Library edit recompiles only the edited component and those after it (seconds to 30 s; ~135 s for CompilerBuiltin). A Java or Scala edit needs `ant compileAll` (~65–75 s), which wipes the caches, so the library is rebuilt once (145–195 s): deliberate in `build.xml`, a different compiler's library, not a repeat.
Skeptic: same worktree after the worker, no `ant`, no library builds. New code `FORTRESS_HOME=W`; old code `FORTRESS_HOME=B` and `FORTRESS_CACHES=W/.old-caches` after `cp -r` of the shared cache; its programs outside B; `FORTRESS_HOME` exported for every command.

Decision offered: after a compiler-only rung the worker could rerun step 8 instead of rebuilding the library (saves 145–195 s), safe only when the change does not affect the library's code generation or type checking; default kept: rebuild.

**Next to try**: skip scalac when no `.scala` file changed (Java-only edits ~70 s to a few seconds; Java signature changes Scala depends on need handling); portable caches by hashing a home-relative path in `NamingCzar.deCaseName` (changes the original tree); time a real `git worktree add` and two agents in parallel; compare re-relocation with a full library rebuild on a real Java-editing rung.

**Files** (in `/home/user/blind-opus/wt-sim/`, nothing committed): `meas/provision.sh`, `mtimesync.py`, `relocate.py`, `libbuild.sh`, `env.sh`; logs `ant0.log`, `ant-w1.log`, `ant-w2.log`, `lib-base.log`; `seed/` the frozen shared cache (33 MB); `w2/` a provisioned worktree; `wt-sim/a` as the earlier attempt left it.

The Opus blinded test also found it, so both tiers solved the problem blind.

- **Opus's answer:** the same one. Copy the build, and relocate one shared library cache: rename each file to its new path's hash and rewrite the paths inside. About 2 seconds per worktree. The skeptic gets no build of its own.
- **Leftover caveat:** its first start, the one your stop killed after 13 minutes, had already built such a relocated cache, which this run found and checked. So that first start found the answer too.
- **One thing Fable didn't find:**
  - A fresh checkout's file dates make the build regenerate 1,071 AST sources after any Java edit.
  - Copying the base tree's file dates onto the worktree avoids it. One Java edit then costs 74 seconds instead of 104.
  - Our seed script stamps dates too, but I haven't checked whether it covers this case.
- **Cost:** about 0.24M tokens over its two starts, and 16 minutes for this run.

What it means for your question: given your goal stated plainly, both tiers solve it in about 15 minutes. So September's "impossible" was not a model that couldn't do it. Why it happened anyway is what the cache archaeology, still running, is digging out.

+## 2. The blinded test, Fable
+## State found in /home/user/blind-fable

+The stopped attempt had finished: `ProjectFortress/build` (4026 classes, 40 MB) plus a complete compiler-library cache (12 MB, 5 jars, analysed 04:43–04:48). It works: `fortress compile` of a 7-line program 3.4 s, `fortress run` 0.6 s. Interpreter caches were empty: `fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss` cold 38.6 s, warm 7.0 s (adds 22 MB of `interpreter*_cache`). No tracked files changed; I removed my two scratch worktrees; the gitignored caches now also hold interpreter entries and a `Smoke1` test.
+## Code facts that decide the design

+- Cache names: `<Name>-<hex>` where hex = Java `String.hashCode()` of the *canonical absolute* source path (`GraphNode` uses `getCanonicalPath()`, so symlinks don't help). A 10-line Python reproduces every name; `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers-d13bcf6` hashes the literal `"ForeignJava"` and is path-independent.

+- Staleness (`GraphRepository.OutOfDateVisitor`): source mtime > cache mtime, plus a *signature* hash of imported Java classes (`ForeignJava.subsetHash`), never class-file mtimes. So a copied build with new mtimes is harmless; a cache copied with **preserved** old mtimes (`cp -p`, `rsync -a`) is older than freshly checked-out sources and forces the 145 s rebuild.

+- `ant compileAll` → `compileCommon` → `cleanCache` deletes `default_repository/caches` (tracked `global.map` included). `ant -Dcache0=/nonexistent -Dcache1=/nonexistent compileAll` neutralises it (verified: cache intact).
+- `FORTRESS_CACHES=<dir>` is honoured by `ProjectProperties` (`fortress.caches` via `StringMap.FromEnv`) and by `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`.
+- `FORTRESS_AUTOHOME` overrides the classpath probing that mis-homes a symlinked build, but ant would still write through the symlink into the shared build — rejected for workers.
+## Designs considered
+1. Symlink/hardlink the build and cache: `cp -al` is 0.05 s, but Java rewrites cache files in place, so hardlinks corrupt the base; symlinked build mis-homes. Rejected.
+2. One shared cache for all worktrees: names differ per path and workers edit the library. Rejected.
+3. **Copy build + copy cache + rename hashes** (workers). Verified.
+4. **Shared read-only base tree + private `FORTRESS_CACHES`** (skeptic's "old code"). Verified.
+## Measured (4 cores)
+- `git worktree add`: 2.0–3.6 s. `cp -r build`: 0.3–1.0 s. `cp -r caches`: 0.04 s. Rename script: 0.05 s (14 renames compiler-only, 56 with interpreter caches).

+- Scratch worktree wt1 seeded this way: compile 3.4 s with `-debug repository 1` showing only the new program as stale; run 0.65 s. wt2 (interpreter caches too): interpreter 9.4 s (vs 38.6 cold), compile 4.0 s.
+- Private cache via `FORTRESS_CACHES` against blind-fable: compile 2.9 s, run 0.6 s, zero writes to the tree's own cache.

+- Worker rebuild in wt1 after touching one Java file, `ant -Dcache0=… -Dcache1=… compileAll`: 99.6 s (fresh checkout makes astgen/operators look out of date, so javac recompiled all 1073 files; scalac is full anyway). Library cache survived; post-rebuild compile 4.6 s, run OK.
+## Recommended recipe
+**Once per batch**, in base tree B at the base commit: `ant compileAll` (80 s), library compile in order (145 s), one interpreter run (39 s) if walk-path rungs exist.
+**Per worker worktree W (~5 s):**
+1. `git worktree add --detach W <base>`
+2. `cp -r B/ProjectFortress/build W/ProjectFortress/build` (no `-p`/`-a`, no links)
+3. `cp -r B/default_repository/caches/. W/default_repository/caches/`

+4. `python3 rehash.py B W W/default_repository/caches` — for each `.fss/.fsi` under `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library`, `ProjectFortress/test_library`, rename `<Name>-<hash(B-path)>.tf[is]` to `<Name>-<hash(W-path)>` in `analyzed_cache`, `analyzed_cache/depends`, `interpreter_cache`, `interpreter_parsed_cache` (script at scratchpad `rehash.py`, 30 lines).
+First program compile 3–4 s; interpreter 9 s.

+**Worker after Java/Scala edits:** `ant -Dcache0=/nonexistent -Dcache1=/nonexistent compileAll` (~100 s, the one unavoidable build). Library-`.fss` edits recompile only the touched component and dependents (mtime); nativeHelpers signature changes auto-recompile CompilerBuiltin. **Caveat:** a compiler change that alters how the library *would* compile (codegen, desugaring) is not detected — such rungs must wipe `*_cache` and redo the 145 s library compile before the skeptic judges.

+**Skeptic:** new code = W as left by the worker (sequential, no copy). Old code = `export FORTRESS_HOME=B FORTRESS_CACHES=$priv` with `cp -r B/default_repository/caches $priv` (0.05 s, no rename since paths are B's); B stays read-only, so any number of skeptics share one base build.
+## Next to try
+- Patch `NamingCzar.deCaseName` to hash a `FORTRESS_AUTOHOME`-relative path: caches become portable, the rename step disappears (changes everyone's cache names once).
+- Touch generated node/operator sources after checkout to skip astgen in the first rebuild (99.6 → ~80 s).
+- Negative controls I inferred from code but did not run: unrenamed cache and `cp -p` copy both forcing the 145 s rebuild.
+- Put per-worktree caches outside `default_repository` via `FORTRESS_CACHES` so even a plain `ant compileAll` cannot wipe them.
+## 3. The blinded test, Opus
+## Recommendation: copy the build, relocate one shared library cache, and give the skeptic no build of its own
+Every timing below was taken while other sessions kept the 4-core machine at a load average of 5–8, so the times are inflated.
+**Designs considered**
+1. Each worktree builds everything itself (61–80 s build, 145–194 s library).
+2. Symlink `ProjectFortress/build` to the base tree's build.
+3. Copy the build and recompile the library cold.
+4. Copy the build and **relocate** the base tree's compiled caches. Recommended.
+5. For old-code runs, use the base tree itself with a private cache directory.
+**What I measured**

+- A no-op `ant compileAll` takes 61 s and is never a no-op: scalac always recompiles every Scala source. `compileAll` depends on `cleanCache`, which deletes `default_repository/caches` (tracked `global.map` included); the first run wiped the earlier attempt's library cache, rebuilt cold in 194 s (AnyType 27, CompilerBuiltin 135, CompilerLibrary 25, CompilerAlgebra 3, CompilerSystem 3.5).
+- Creating a worktree (separate-index checkout as a stand-in for `git worktree add`): 1.6 s, 222 MB. Copying the 40 MB build: 0.17–0.3 s.

+- Trap: checkout mtimes make `Fortress.ast` look newer than the generated AST sources and the copied `OperatorStuffGenerator.class` newer than `Operators.java`; one edited Java file then cost 104 s (1,071 AST sources regenerated identically, 1,073 files recompiled).

+- Fix: copy the base tree's mtimes onto the tracked files (0.17 s for 10,506 files), then `cp -a` the build and `.dependencies`: the same one-file edit cost 74 s, 1 file compiled, nothing regenerated; the remaining ~60 s is scalac.

+- Relocation: rename each cache file with the new path's hash and rewrite the embedded absolute paths, over the analysed, interpreter and interpreter-parsed caches, `bytecode_cache` and `nativewrapper_cache` copied unchanged: 0.1–0.3 s. In the relocated worktree: compile 3.4–4.6 s, run 0.7 s, interpreter 9 s, no library cache file rewritten. Without it: interpreter first run 38 s, compiler path 145–194 s library build.

+- Library edits are incremental: a comment added to `CompilerLibrary.fss` recompiled CompilerLibrary 30 s, CompilerAlgebra 1.3 s, CompilerSystem 2.2 s; CompilerBuiltin and AnyType untouched (cold: 194 s).
+- Old-code runs: `FORTRESS_HOME=<base>` plus `FORTRESS_CACHES=<private copy of the shared cache>` (0.01 s, no relocation); compile 3.4 s, run 0.7 s; base cache md5-identical before and after.

+- Symlinked build confirmed broken without `FORTRESS_AUTOHOME` (a compile wrote into the base tree's cache); with it, `ant` in the worktree would still write through the symlink. Copying costs 0.2 s, so a symlink saves nothing.
+**Recommended recipe**

+Once per batch, in base tree B at the base commit (4–5 min, only when the base changed): 1. `ant compileAll` (61–80 s; step 2 must follow). 2. Library compile in the fixed order (145–194 s). 3. content.text:
The cache archaeology has reported. Together with the two blinded tests, it answers your question of this morning. All three are filed in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`.

**Who said it was impossible:** Opus 5, on 09-17.
- A review worker measured something true: cache file names contain a hash of the source path, so a plain copy is cold.
- It wrote that as "cannot be copied into a worktree".
- Its coordinator told you: "A worktree cannot be given a warm cache — at all."
- Neither ever tried copying and renaming. The reason they gave, the path in the file name, is exactly what renaming fixes.

**Who carried it after:** every tier, unexamined.
- The Fable 5.1 coordinator and 18 Fable 5.1 workers had it in their reading; none was asked about it.
- On 09-30 I, on Opus 5.5, told you it "was tried" and widened it to "cannot take the build either". That was wrong.
- It lived in INDEX, the plan and the script's prefix, never in FACTS, so no rule ever prompted a re-check.

**Your signals:** nine, from 08-27 to 10-02. Most were answered narrower than you meant:
- Your "reuse the cached library" was heard as a question about invalidation.
- The cache probe you asked for died in 56 seconds and was never re-run.
- Your "Duh!" to "copying a built tree" got no answer.
- On 10-02 you named the mechanism yourself. It was built within 23 minutes and took about 30 minutes of engineering.

**Would Opus 5.5 give up too?** Not when the goal is stated plainly. Both tiers found the renaming answer blind in about 15 minutes. Their brief gave them the path-hash fact and your goal, though, so it doesn't test discovery without that framing.

**So the failure was process, not capability:**
- a measured fact written up as an impossibility
- a probe that died and was never re-run
- questions narrowed to pricing
- no estimate of what rebuilding in every worktree would cost over all the batches to come
- later agents citing the record instead of asking again

Still owed from this morning: the rule on engineering taste, drafted from this evidence. Briefly: an obstacle gets an attempt to engineer around it, and an estimate of its recurring cost, before it is accepted as impossible. I'll bring you the draft.
